entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Edward the Confessor was the last King of the English from 1042 until his death in 1066. He was born in 1003 and succeeded his half-brother, Harold Harefoot, as the ruler of the House of Wessex.

A member of the House of Normandy, Edward's reign saw the beginning of a new era in English history, marked by the consolidation of power, the development of the English Church, and the preparation for the Norman Conquest. He was canonized by Pope Alexander II in 1165, recognizing his piety and devotion to the Church.

Edward's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, influencing the course of English history and shaping the nation's identity. His reign marked a turning point between the Anglo-Saxon and Norman periods, setting the stage for the eventual union of England and Normandy under a single ruler.

The passing of Edward the Confessor in 1066 triggered a succession crisis that led to the events of the Norman Conquest, with Harold Godwinson being crowned king just days later.

A key figure in English history, Edward's impact on the country's politics, religion, and culture remains significant to this day.
